title: DOSH Adds Google Pay to Extend Digital Wallets to Underbanked Users
snippet: The FCA-regulated prepaid account, built for financially excluded consumers, now supports contactless Android payments without a credit check. The post DOSH Adds Google Pay to Extend Digital Wallets to Underbanked Users appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
DOSH, the prepaid Mastercard account operated by Hereford-based payment specialist allpay Ltd, has added Google Pay support for its Android customers. Eligible users can now add their DOSH card to Google Wallet and make contactless payments in stores, in apps and online wherever the Google Pay logo is accepted, including through compatible Android smartwatches.

The move is targeted explicitly at consumers who are unbanked, underbanked or otherwise excluded from mainstream financial products. DOSH is credit-check-free and carries no overdraft facility, positioning it as a spending-control tool rather than a credit instrument. The Google Pay integration gives those customers access to the same contactless payment rails used widely across the UK without requiring them to hold a current account at a high-street bank.

Tony Killeen, founder and entrepreneur of allpay, said: “People who are unbanked, underbanked or financially excluded should not be left with fewer choices or outdated ways to pay. Bringing Google Pay to DOSH helps open a modern payment experience while preserving the control and transparency that our customers value.”

The mechanics and security case

From a technical standpoint, the integration uses Google Pay’s standard tokenisation model: the customer’s physical card number is not transmitted to the retailer at the point of sale. Instead, a device-specific token handles the transaction, adding a layer of protection that is comparable to what a standard bank-issued debit card provides through the same wallet. This matters for the target demographic, where loss of a physical card can cause acute disruption to day-to-day spending.

The DOSH account also supports real-time push notifications and an in-app card lock, features that complement the digital wallet by keeping the customer in control of a balance that cannot go negative. Cash access remains available through up to 11,500 Post Office branches across the UK, which sustains optionality for customers who move between digital and cash-based spending.

Market context and regulatory backdrop

The timing of the announcement sits against a data point worth noting. A February 2025 feedback statement from the Financial Conduct Authority and the Payment Systems Regulator recorded that the share of UK card transactions completed via a digital wallet rose from eight per cent in 2019 to twenty-nine per cent in 2023. That structural shift means the gap between what a mainstream bank customer experiences and what an excluded consumer can access has been widening, even as the technology has become ubiquitous.

Several prepaid and e-money providers already operate in the financially excluded segment in the UK, including Pockit, Suits Me and card programmes run through credit unions. The competitive question for DOSH is distribution: the product reaches customers partly through local authorities, community partners and social housing providers rather than purely through direct-to-consumer channels, which is a differentiated model that could support lower acquisition costs and higher trust among hard-to-reach cohorts.

allpay holds FCA authorisation as an electronic money institution under registration number 900539. That regulatory status means DOSH sits within the e-money framework rather than the deposit-taking regime, so customer balances are not covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme but must be safeguarded in a segregated account in line with the Electronic Money Regulations 2011. Prospective users and partner organisations should note that distinction.

The next indicators to watch are uptake rates among DOSH’s existing customer base and whether the Google Pay capability accelerates take-up through the social-housing and local-authority distribution channels. An Apple Pay equivalent for iOS users has not been announced.

title: The Autumn Budget 2026 – How FinTech holds the answers to Burnham’s biggest problems
snippet: UK FinTech urges the government to back SME lending, AI in financial services, investment and sterling stablecoins in the upcoming Budget to drive growth, jobs and financial inclusion nationwide. The post The Autumn Budget 2026 – How FinTech holds the answers to Burnham’s biggest problems appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Ahead of the first Budget of the Burnham government, the UK FinTech community has a clear message for the Chancellor: our sector is one of the most important allies in helping this government achieve its ambition around driving good growth in every postcode.

For more than a decade, the innovative tools and services created by UK FinTech have had a profoundly positive impact on the lives of everyday people. Whether it is supporting first-time home buyers, helping hard working people grow their savings and make their money work better for them, helping families navigate the cost of living crisis, or putting financial education at people’s fingertips, FinTech is delivering tangible economic and social impact across the country.

More than 68% of all SME lending across the country is today being done by challenger banks and alternative lenders – FinTech is truly powering up the engine of our UK economy. Moreover, FinTech is the subsector of financial services which continually sees the highest level of job creation, driving growth in every corner of the UK.

And despite the repeated economic headwinds we have faced as a nation over the past decade, FinTech has remained one of the UK’s true and undisputed growth success stories on both the domestic and global stage. It is a prime example of a sector where collaboration between industry, government and regulators have enabled the UK to be genuinely world-leading – we have secured more investment into FinTech than any other country in the world bar the United States, and we far surpass our European peers.

FinTech has already proven itself as a tremendous force for good for the UK, driving hugely positive impact to families and small businesses across the country – and we stand at the ready to deliver even more.

This Budget is the opportunity for the Government to back our thriving sector and enable it to deliver even further benefits. To achieve this, we need to see four core policy priorities being progressed:

Unlock more finance for SMEs through challenger banks

We recommend that the Government commissions the PRA to launch a holistic review of bank capital requirements to ensure proportionate treatment of challenger banks. More immediately, we recommend the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge threshold rise from £100 million to £500 million, to promote retail competition, support UK listings, and boost SME lending across the country.

 Make the UK the world leader in AI in financial services by 2030

The UK has a unique opportunity to combine its pro-innovation approach to AI with its leadership in Open Banking and Smart Data to become a world leader in trusted agentic commerce and finance. We recommend the Government brings forward the legal and regulatory basis for Open Finance, and prioritises AI-enabled financial guidance, savings, investments and SME finance as the first use cases, by the end of 2026.

 Strengthen the UK’s talent, investment and entrepreneurial ecosystem

The Budget is an opportunity to modernise employee share ownership so high-growth FinTechs can compete for talent with Big Tech and incumbent banks, by expanding Enterprise Management Incentives (EMI) eligibility and limits and reforming Company Share Option Plans (CSOPs). Government should also introduce a Scale-up Reinvestment Relief and abolish stamp duty on UK listed shares to boost reinvestment by founders and domestic investment. Together, these measures could unlock over £1 billion in additional investment in UK FinTech and up to £250 billion in UK listed equity demand.

 Establish the UK as a global leader in sterling stablecoins

At this Budget, the Government should offer clear and unambiguous support for Sterling stablecoins through a coordinated strategy that treats regulated stablecoins as cash-equivalent digital money and ensures a level playing field with other forms of digital money. This should include updating accounting standards and committing to accept stablecoins as payment for Government services and tax.

UK FinTech is already delivering the Government’s ambition for good growth: creating skilled jobs, attracting investment, and expanding access to financial services for businesses and individuals in every postcode. This Budget is an opportunity to build on that success, for the benefit of consumers and small businesses across the country.

title: Circle and Proof Demo Verified-ID Stablecoin Payments for AI Agents
snippet: The two firms are combining Proof's x401 identity protocol with Circle's USDC Agent Wallets to let merchants trust and settle AI agent purchases. The post Circle and Proof Demo Verified-ID Stablecoin Payments for AI Agents appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Circle Internet Group (NYSE: CRCL) and identity infrastructure firm Proof have unveiled a collaboration at Money20/20 in Las Vegas last week, demonstrating how verified legal identity and stablecoin payments can be combined in a single agent-initiated transaction. The demo addresses one of the more pressing structural problems in agentic commerce: merchants currently have no reliable way to know who authorised a purchase made by an AI agent, leaving them to choose between blocking agents outright or accepting the associated fraud and chargeback risk.

How the protocols fit together

Pat Kinsel, founder and chief executive of Proof

The integration draws on two open HTTP-layer standards. Proof’s x401 protocol, published in June 2026 and moved into production last week, uses the HTTP 401 “Unauthorised” response to let a merchant specify what identity proof it requires and which credential issuers it trusts. Circle’s x402 protocol uses the HTTP 402 “Payment Required” response to specify how the agent should pay. Used in sequence, x401 answers who the agent acts for, and x402 answers how it settles the transaction.

In the demo flow, a merchant responds to an inbound agent request with both an x401 identity requirement and an x402 USDC payment request. The agent’s Proof wallet presents a verified credential derived from identity proofing certified to NIST IAL2 standard, accompanied by a signed, purchase-specific approval. Only the relevant identity facts are disclosed; no full ID document is transmitted or stored by the merchant. The agent then pays from a Circle Agent Wallet in USDC over x402. The merchant retains signed, tamper-evident evidence of who authorised the transaction, which can be used in dispute resolution without requiring Proof to be called again in real time.

A secondary mechanism embedded in the protocol stack is commercially notable. Proof prices identity claims individually, and the same x402 channel can route a micropayment from the merchant to the identity issuer for each verification used. That removes the bilateral contract requirement that has historically limited the reuse of verified identity across ecosystems: a merchant can pay for a check on the spot, at the moment it needs it, without a prior sales relationship with the credential issuer.

Pat Kinsel, founder and chief executive of Proof, said: “Our demo with Circle shows one exchange can answer both questions: verified identity from Proof and payment in USDC. That gives businesses a reason to say yes to agents instead of blocking them.”

Market context and regulatory read-across

The timing is pointed. Several large institutions at Money20/20 are understood to be blocking AI agent traffic entirely, a posture that carries its own commercial cost as consumer adoption of AI assistants accelerates. The Proof and Circle approach is one of several competing frameworks attempting to resolve agentic identity, alongside emerging work in the W3C verifiable credentials ecosystem and proprietary agent-authentication layers from payment networks and cloud providers.

From a regulatory perspective, the NIST IAL2 credential anchor is significant. That standard is referenced in US federal identity frameworks and is gaining traction in Know Your Customer discussions as a benchmark for remote identity proofing. In the UK, the Digital Identity and Attributes Trust Framework published by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology sets comparable requirements, suggesting that a credential meeting IAL2 could attract recognition in cross-border contexts. The European eIDAS 2.0 wallet framework similarly defines trust levels against which x401-type presentations could eventually be assessed. Whether regulators will accept protocol-layer identity assertions as satisfying KYC obligations under anti-money laundering rules remains an open question, and one that will shape how quickly financial institutions can adopt agent-native payment flows rather than routing them through existing customer-authenticated channels.

title: Ownera and Utila Partner to Broaden Institutional Digital Asset Stack
snippet: The two firms will offer a joint solution spanning custody, wallet infrastructure, tokenisation and blockchain connectivity for financial institutions. The post Ownera and Utila Partner to Broaden Institutional Digital Asset Stack appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Ownera and Utila have announced a strategic partnership aimed at giving financial institutions, corporate treasuries and enterprise clients access to a wider range of digital asset infrastructure through a single coordinated framework. The deal was announced on 8 October 2026.

The partnership brings together two distinct capability sets. Ownera contributes its FinP2P network and SuperApps Platform, which the company says orchestrates more than $5 billion in monthly trading volume across multiple chains, legacy ledgers and counterparties. Utila contributes wallet infrastructure, multi-party computation security controls and governance tooling, and reports processing more than $35 billion in monthly volume across more than 350 institutional clients. Together, the companies say they intend to offer a joined-up solution across custody operations, wallet management, tokenised asset interoperability and blockchain application delivery.

Neither company disclosed commercial terms, revenue-sharing arrangements or whether the partnership carries exclusivity provisions.

The strategic rationale

Ami Ben-David, founder and CEO at Ownera

The core problem the partnership is designed to address is fragmentation. Institutions that want to add tokenised asset capabilities typically face a patchwork of specialist vendors: one for custody, one for interoperability, one for wallet governance, one for settlement rails. Each integration carries its own technical overhead and compliance review. A pre-integrated stack that spans those layers reduces friction and shortens the procurement cycle, which is a meaningful commercial argument for enterprise buyers who are cautious about committing engineering resource to digital asset pilots.

Bentzi Rabi, co-founder and CEO at Utila

Ami Ben-David, founder and chief executive of Ownera, said: “Through our partnership with Utila, we look forward to expanding blockchain operations from siloed pilot use cases to institutional applications.” Bentzi Rabi, co-founder and chief executive of Utila, added that institutions need secure infrastructure to manage digital assets and transact across different networks “while retaining control over their assets and transactions.”

Market context

The partnership fits a broader pattern of vendor consolidation in the institutional digital asset infrastructure segment. Several well-capitalised providers, including Fireblocks, Copper and BitGo, already offer custody, wallet and policy-control capabilities as a bundle, and custody-to-interoperability integration is an area of active product development across the sector. The competitive question for Ownera and Utila is whether a contractual partnership delivers the same integration depth and support continuity that a fully unified product would offer. Enterprise procurement teams at regulated institutions typically prefer a single contractual counterparty and a single SLA, which a partnership structure does not automatically guarantee.

Regulatory tailwinds are relevant context. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, which came into full effect for asset-referenced tokens in 2024, has raised the bar for custody and operational controls for institutions operating in European markets. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority‘s digital assets regime remains under development, but the direction of travel, towards mandatory custody segregation and robust governance, aligns with the capability set both firms are marketing. For institutions already navigating that compliance build-out, a pre-integrated infrastructure offering carries a clearer value proposition than it would have done three years ago.

The near-term milestones to watch are whether the two firms announce a named joint client, whether the collaboration produces a co-developed product or remains at the referral and integration layer, and how the partnership evolves as the UK and EU regulatory frameworks for digital asset custody and interoperability continue to mature.

snippet: The companies are extending their partnership to provide financial firms with the infrastructure needed to issue stablecoin-funded cards.

                Dive Brief
        

                

The companies are extending their partnership to provide financial firms with the infrastructure needed to issue stablecoin-funded cards.

        

            

        Published Oct. 26, 2026

Dive Brief:

Euronet, the international payments infrastructure provider, and Fireblocks, the digital asset infrastructure company, are collaborating to enable banks, fintech and other financial firms to create their own stablecoin-funded card offerings, Euronet said in a press release.

Financial firms that use Euronet’s Ren and CoreCard issuing services can now access Fireblock’s embedded wallet infrastructure that holds and transfers stablecoins, the Oct. 19 release said. 

The companies are providing the service as a white-label offering that financial firms can integrate into their own banking and mobile wallet apps, per the release.

Dive Insight:

Through the partnership, Euronet and Fireblocks aim to bring stablecoin card programs into new markets and bridge the gap between digital assets and traditional card payments, the release said. The two previously partnered last year to offer settlement and pre-funding services for cross-border payments, per the release. 

“A decade ago, stablecoins were just a trader’s tool to exit Bitcoin,” Fireblock’s chief payments and network officer, Ran Goldi, said in a release. “Today, combined with global cards, they are the ideal off-ramp for digital assets.”

Along with Euronet and Fireblocks, other major payments players, including card network Visa and processor Fiserv, as well as startups, are also eyeing the stablecoin market. 

Earlier this month, MassPay, the Las Vegas-based direct payments company, said it teamed up with Block’s Cash App to provide a real-time payments service to those digital wallet account holders. 

In a September interview, MassPay CEO Ran Grushkowsky said the company, which uses digital asset technology to provide payments to gig workers, contractors and marketplace sellers, has seen “growing demand for stablecoins, primarily by large-scale institutions that feel comfortable due to some clearance in the regulation.”

Meanwhile, Rain, the stablecoin infrastructure company, joined money transfer company Western Union’s digital asset network last year and locked arms with its rival MoneyGram in September. Rain enables corporate clients to integrate its digital asset technology into their architecture. 

As startups vie for digital asset clientele, established payments providers have been racing to integrate stablecoins into traditional finance. 

In July, a consortium of about 140 companies, including payments giants like Visa and digital payments provider Stripe, convened to launch the Open USD stablecoin. 

The following month, Visa and its smaller competitor Mastercard joined forces with Circle Internet Group to support Arc, an initiative that seeks to underpin stablecoin transactions in financial markets, real-time payments and agentic commerce.

Though some newcomers and established payments companies alike are working to bring stablecoins into the mainstream financial system, others are wary of embracing the technology. 

A Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank survey of 148 companies in its district found that financial firms aren’t embracing stablecoins, because of their satisfaction with current payment methods; little demand from customers; and a lack of familiarity with the digital asset class.

title: Settling cross-border payments remains tough
snippet: Global payments are moving faster, but local settlement remains a pain point for many companies, according to speakers on a Money20/20 panel.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Global payments are moving faster, but local settlement remains a pain point for many companies, according to speakers on a Money20/20 panel.

        

            

        Published Oct. 29, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                An exhibition hall sign greeted attendees at the 2026 Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.
            
        
            Justin Bachman/Payments Dive
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Settlement of a cross-border payment at its destination remains a pain point across the industry, despite improvements in rails, speed and interoperability among players, payments executives said last week in a panel discussion.

The last portion of a cross-border payment accounts for 80% of the total speed of a transaction, regardless of the payment rail or instrument that is used, said Leigh Amaro, Americas CEO for Swift, the digital financial messaging firm for international payments. Amaro spoke about how cross-border payments are evolving on Oct. 20 at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.

Given current regulations, “an instrument can leave one country looking like one thing and completely end up in another's jurisdiction looking completely different,” Debopama Sen, Citigroup’s head of payments and services, said during the discussion. “And then when you marry that with regulatory cross-border restriction challenges, the last mile is where our clients struggle, and the last mile does need to be addressed.”

Dive Insight:

Cross-border payments totaled about $190 trillion last year, generating about $290 billion in revenue for the payments industry, according to an August report from the consulting firm McKinsey.

Three-quarters of Swift-enabled payments reach the recipient’s beneficiary bank within 10 minutes, Amaro said. At that point, however, local rules, operating hours and other challenges slow the settlement process, regardless of whether a payment was sent via stablecoin, tokenized deposit or a traditional rail, she said.

Meanwhile, regulators in many countries are pushing for more price transparency with respect to the services, while compliance complexity has increased due to newer fintech entrants into the cross-border arena, the McKinsey report noted.

Some of the costs and complexities of cross-border payments are slowly decreasing, threatening to commoditize the field, said Jonathan Zell, a McKinsey partner in the consulting firm’s payments practice, who moderated the session.

Kush Saxena, CEO of Banking Circle Group, a Luxembourg-based fintech that specializes in cross-border payments, challenged that contention, drawing a distinction between cash and data transfers.

“I wouldn’t say moving money is a commodity. I think moving data is becoming easier,” Saxena said, noting “a ton of interoperability” the industry has created above the fiat level. “When it comes to fiat, you get into sort of regulated territory, and … there is a 180-degree divide between where global commerce is going and between where regulators are going.”

One area that Citi and other banks are working to solve is “bridging the world of blockchain and digital assets with the fiat world” in cross-border payments, Sen said. She said Citi clients have been seeking this capability “because they’re not really looking at it, saying, ‘Hey, I want to use that technology.’ They’re saying, ‘Can you solve my problem?’”

Last month, Citibank introduced a cross-border, instant-payment service, using its global network and collaborating with Swift, to help customers avoid the need for local banking relationships.

“Data can move at the speed of light, but that’s not enough. The cash has to be available,” Sen said, noting the success of the M-Pesa money-transfer service in Africa due to its abundant cash-payout locations in each country.

title: Finery Markets: 100 days of MiCA and the Execution Gap Banks Must Close
snippet: Finery Markets says 89% of banks now budget for digital assets, yet trading infrastructure remains the missing piece a year on. The post Finery Markets: 100 days of MiCA and the Execution Gap Banks Must Close appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
One hundred days after MiCA’s 1 July registration deadline, the headline number, 280 firms on ESMA‘s initial list, down from 2,747 operating under national transitional regimes in 2024, turns out to be the less consequential data point. According to two reports published by institutional crypto trading infrastructure firm Finery Markets in October 2026, the structural shift playing out underneath the compliance story is about liquidity, not headcount.

EURC, the euro-denominated stablecoin issued by Circle, saw volume on the Finery Markets platform rise 46 times year on year in the first nine months of 2026. Yet it still accounts for just 0.12% of total stablecoin flow through the network. Euro stablecoin supply has grown 22.6% this year to approximately $848 million, while dollar-denominated supply has been flat. The figures confirm MiCA opened a race to build native euro liquidity that remains, as the report puts it, a test of volume rather than availability.

The OTC data behind the first report covers 16 million institutional spot trades across nine months. OTC volume grew 57% year on year while the top 20 centralised exchanges collectively lost 47% of comparable activity. Stablecoins now account for 83% of trades on the network. Contributors include Banking Circle, Fipto, The Vault and identity and compliance firm Sumsub.

The execution layer banks have not built

The second report, focused on bank strategy, finds that 89% of banks have an active budget for digital assets, but only 16% have anything in production. Of the largest institutions surveyed, JPMorgan, Citi, BNY, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Standard Chartered, Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, BBVA and Revolut, nearly every live product runs on third-party rails. Custody, tokenised deposits and exchange-traded product access have been delivered. Trading has not.

That gap is the commercial proposition underlying the Finery Markets release. The firm argues that custody addresses a security question, not a revenue one. The client request that follows custody is the ability to trade held assets without routing them to an exchange the bank does not control. Building that internally requires separate bilateral liquidity relationships, each carrying its own credit agreement, fragmented pricing that complicates best-execution obligations, and a settlement infrastructure build measured in quarters rather than weeks.

Finery Markets’ alternative is a non-custodial connection to firm liquidity across more than 200 crypto and fiat pairs, with automated netting, role-based access controls and a full audit trail. Two deployment models are offered: a white-label master account in which the bank remains the regulated counterparty, and a full white-label network in which clients trade with one another and the bank typically avoids the capital requirements of a broker-dealer licence.

Regulatory context and platform updates

The regulatory read-across is substantial. In the US, the OCC has granted 16 digital asset trust charters in ten months. The GENIUS Act, MiCA, the UK’s evolving digital assets regime and Basel III capital treatment of crypto exposures are all shaping what banks can offer and at what cost. Roughly one fifth of the current MiCA register is now composed of banks, which reflects an appetite but also a compliance overhead that smaller specialist CASPs have been faster to absorb.

Finery Markets also disclosed two platform updates this month. The connectivity hub now allows institutional participants to store exchange API credentials directly within the platform interface, integrating price discovery from venues covering what the firm describes as more than two thirds of global crypto liquidity. The white-label stack has been updated with embedded API documentation, which the company says has reduced client integration timelines by a factor of 18.7 compared with a prior baseline, a figure it attributes to an AI-assisted integration repository. The 18.7 multiplier is not independently benchmarked in the release.

The firm also co-hosted a private luncheon at TOKEN2049 Singapore with Caladan, Utila and Stablecoin Insider, drawing approximately 150 professionals from OTC trading, market making, payments and stablecoin infrastructure. The consensus from those conversations, as reported by Finery Markets, was that firms growing fastest are treating routing, settlement and prefunding as infrastructure decisions rather than operational workarounds.

title: KR1 plc Launches Dedicated Ethereum Validators via Lido stVaults
snippet: The LSE-listed onchain infrastructure firm is staking over 6,200 ETH through a dedicated Lido stVault operated by P2P.org. The post KR1 plc Launches Dedicated Ethereum Validators via Lido stVaults appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
KR1 plc, the only dedicated onchain infrastructure company listed on the Main Market of the London Stock Exchange, has launched its own dedicated Ethereum validators, beginning the deployment of a 6,200 ETH position worth more than £10 million at current levels. The validators run inside a dedicated Lido stVault, operated by institutional staking provider P2P.org.

The move delivers on operational commitments set out in the company’s October 2025 Prospectus and marks a structural shift in how KR1 manages its Ethereum holdings. Rather than participating in a commingled staking pool, the company now controls its own vault settings, including deposits and withdrawals, the validator fee arrangement, and the option to mint stETH for liquidity on demand.

The deal

The launch begins with ten active validators, with plans to scale beyond one hundred. Full deployment of the 6,200 ETH position will be paced by Ethereum’s validator entry queue, which determines how quickly new validators can be activated on the network. By operating dedicated validators rather than delegating to a shared pool, KR1 says it achieves clearer income attribution and retains a higher proportion of staking rewards net of fees.

Managing Directors and Co-Founders George McDonaugh and Keld van Schreven described the milestone as central to KR1’s operating strategy: “This gives public-market investors a clearly attributed route into the infrastructure income at the centre of KR1’s operating strategy, while reinforcing our position as the only dedicated infrastructure operator on the London Stock Exchange Main Market.”

KR1 was a seed investor in Lido, making the commercial relationship a downstream use of an existing portfolio position.

Amir Kahoori, Ethereum Senior Product Manager at P2P.org, noted that accountability differs materially between a dedicated validator set and a shared pool: “The uptime, the slashing record and the per validator reporting all come from the operator. stVaults unlock optional liquidity on top of the validators, without commingling funds in a pool.”

Market context

The launch sits within a broader trend of institutional and listed-company capital moving onto proof-of-stake networks and demanding infrastructure-grade controls rather than retail-style pooled products. Listed vehicles such as MicroStrategy established the template for balance-sheet digital asset holdings; KR1’s approach extends that to productive yield-generating infrastructure, which carries additional complexity around reporting, slashing risk and liquidity management.

Lido remains the dominant liquid-staking middleware by total value locked on Ethereum, though it has faced scrutiny over decentralisation and governance concentration. The stVault architecture, which allows institutions to run a branded, segregated set of validators while accessing the Lido protocol’s stETH liquidity token, is positioned by Lido as its institutional-grade answer to those concerns. Kean Gilbert, Head of Institutional Relations at the Lido Ecosystem Foundation, said KR1 is the first publicly listed company to launch its own branded validators on stVaults.

From a regulatory standpoint, Ethereum staking income is increasingly in scope for treatment as a financial product in several jurisdictions. In the EU, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) does not directly address staking rewards, but the European Securities and Markets Authority has signalled ongoing review of liquid staking tokens. In the UK, the FCA has not yet issued final guidance on staking, though its 2023 crypto asset financial promotions regime requires careful framing of yield claims. For KR1, operating as a listed company with a corporate broker and regulated financial adviser, the public-market disclosure obligations add a further layer of compliance discipline that distinguishes its position from that of unlisted staking aggregators.

The near-term metrics to watch are the rate at which KR1 scales its validator count toward the 100-plus target, the net staking yield it reports against the benchmark of pooled alternatives, and whether similar listed vehicles follow with comparable dedicated-validator structures.

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

          

          

        

              

                  

On this page

AI adoption: good and poor practice

From frontier AI to agentic finance

Becoming an agentic regulator

Conclusion

The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering.

  

            						

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'

In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.

Notes to editors

The FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.

The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

fullText:
Global financial services group LuLu Financial Holdings (LFH) has partnered with fintech infrastructure provider Purpleplum to overhaul commercial banking and payment delivery for UAE businesses. Under the collaboration, Purpleplum’s core-agnostic orchestration platform will power LuLu Money Business—LFH’s dedicated SME and enterprise financial proposition.

The partnership integrates existing banking rails, payment networks, and operational workflows into a single interface. The agreement was formalized in the presence of Adeeb Ahamed, managing director of LuLu Financial Holdings, alongside Purpleplum co-founders Kalyan Karteek Sadasivuni and Sai Sandeep Sadasivuni.

Integrated Banking with Agentic AI Onboarding

The initial phase of the rollout establishes a comprehensive digital banking suite for small and medium-sized enterprises. Central to this deployment are digital business accounts issued in partnership with ruya, an Islamic digital bank licensed and regulated by the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE).

Through a unified application layer, LuLu Money Business brings together several operational capabilities:

Digital Islamic Accounts: Direct issuance of business accounts via ruya, providing fully regulated corporate banking infrastructure.

Agentic AI Onboarding: Digital account opening managed by autonomous AI workflows, with thousands of commercial applications currently in review.

Payroll & Compliance Rails: Native integration of the UAE’s Wages Protection System (WPS) and automated salary administration, building upon LuLu Exchange’s corporate payroll network.

Commercial Payments & Cards: Consolidated payment tools, corporate expense cards, and global remittances powered by LFH’s cross-border settlement infrastructure.

The deployment targets an underserved segment that forms the backbone of the domestic economy. According to data from the UAE Ministry of Economy and Tourism, small and medium-sized enterprises represent nearly 95 per cent of all businesses in the country. Across approximately 1.33 million registered SMEs, the sector generates 63 per cent of national GDP and sustains more than 85 per cent of private-sector employment.

“With LuLu Money Business, our focus is on making everyday financial services simpler, more connected and easier to manage for SMEs,” stated Adeeb Ahamed. “Through our partnership with Purpleplum, we are combining its modular, core-agnostic orchestration platform with our existing infrastructure to modernise how these services are delivered and unlock greater value from established financial rails. This gives us the flexibility to introduce new capabilities over time, deepen our financial relationships with businesses and expand what LuLu Money Business can offer as their needs evolve.”

Fintech Orchestration and Regional Roadmaps

Purpleplum’s modular technology enables financial institutions to deploy digital banking, Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS), and embedded finance without replacing underlying legacy cores. To date, the platform supports 1.1 million active users and has cleared more than 520 million transactions.

“The Middle East is rapidly redefining the future of digital banking, driven by progressive regulation, forward-thinking institutions and a strong appetite for technological advancement,” noted Kalyan Karteek Sadasivuni, co-founder and managing director of Purpleplum. “By combining AI-first banking infrastructure with a strong on-ground presence and local team, we aim to be a long-term technology and infrastructure partner for regional banks, fintechs and enterprises looking to build, launch and scale modern financial products faster.”

As part of its regional strategy, Purpleplum will establish the UAE as its operating base over the next 12 to 24 months, focusing on expanding local partnerships and deploying AI-native workflows spanning automated underwriting, trade finance, and corporate lending.

For LuLu Financial Holdings—which operates physical and digital channels across more than ten countries in the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent, and the Asia-Pacific region—the platform architecture has been engineered for international scalability. Following the UAE rollout, LFH plans to expand the LuLu Money Business proposition across the GCC, India, and APAC, with future iterations incorporating working-capital lending, trade financing, receivables management, and automated treasury services.

title: TransferGo and UNITED24 Launch Ukraine Student Charity Transfer Campaign
snippet: TransferGo is donating 0.2% of every transfer to a Ukrainian IBAN to UNITED24's education fund until 29 October. The post TransferGo and UNITED24 Launch Ukraine Student Charity Transfer Campaign appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TransferGo has launched a time-limited charitable campaign with UNITED24, the Ukrainian government’s official fundraising platform, under the banner “Transfers That Unite”. Until 29 October 2026, the remittance company will contribute an additional 0.2% of every transfer sent to a Ukrainian IBAN to UNITED24’s Education and Science programme, at no extra cost to the sender.

The campaign is framed around supporting Ukrainian students enrolled at domestic colleges, a population that has faced sustained disruption since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The BigThings 2.0 event

To mark the initiative, TransferGo held its BigThings 2.0 event in Warsaw on 10 October, drawing nearly 150 attendees, including more than 100 Ukrainian content creators based across Poland. Influencers travelled from Krakow, Poznan, Wroclaw, Gdansk, Lublin and Szczecin for an event the company described as combining community networking with practical guidance on growing digital audiences.

The guest of honour was Ukrainian singer Kateryna Pavlenko, known professionally as MONOKATE, who spoke about the cultural value of Ukrainian-language content and performed a short acoustic set. Valentyna Kuzmin, Vice Consul of the Consulate General of Ukraine in Krakow, also attended. The format echoed TransferGo’s previous community events: a first BigThings gathering in Warsaw in 2025 and a TRUE INFLUENCE event for Ukrainian creators held in Prague this spring.

Krzysztof Szatecki, Brand and Demand Director at TransferGo, said: “Ukrainian creators abroad have become some of the strongest voices keeping Ukraine’s story alive, and BigThings 2.0 was our way of bringing those voices into one room. Every transfer home is already an act of care for family, and with Transfers That Unite, we’re making sure that it also helps the next generation of Ukrainian professionals finish their studies.”

Market and regulatory context

Remittance corridors to Ukraine have been a significant commercial focus for cross-border payment providers since 2022. Ukraine became one of the world’s largest remittance-receiving economies as its diaspora expanded, and several fintech firms have competed for a share of the Polish-to-Ukraine corridor in particular. TransferGo, which says it serves more than nine million customers across 160 countries and has operated for 14 years, counts the Ukrainian diaspora as a core demographic.

The “Transfers That Unite” mechanism, in which a fraction of a commercial transaction fee is redirected to a charitable fund, is an established model in the remittance sector. It sidesteps the friction of asking senders to make a separate donation while generating measurable social impact data that can be used in brand positioning. The 0.2% contribution rate is modest on individual transactions but can aggregate meaningfully across a high-volume corridor.

UNITED24, launched by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in May 2022, reported cumulative fundraising of more than $3.9 billion from donors in over 145 countries as of the date of the release. The platform operates across several programme areas; the Education and Science strand is the recipient of this campaign’s proceeds.

For TransferGo, the initiative also serves as a community-building exercise among diaspora influencers, a distribution channel for brand awareness in a segment where trust and peer recommendation matter more than traditional advertising. The effectiveness of that channel will depend on how actively the creator network promotes the campaign before the 29 October close date.

title: NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK Join CFIT Financial Inclusion Coalition
snippet: Three major UK banks have backed CFIT's coalition to develop a Supported Payments framework for people who need help managing money without ceding full The post NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK Join CFIT Financial Inclusion Coalition appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
NatWest, Nationwide and HSBC UK have confirmed participation in the Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology‘s Financial Inclusion Coalition, announced on 15 October 2026. The coalition is developing a Supported Payments framework intended to create a legally recognised middle ground between full financial independence and formal arrangements such as Lasting Power of Attorney or deputyship.

The move follows HM Treasury‘s Economic Secretary welcoming the initiative at the Fintech as a Force for Good conference in London the previous week, underlining a degree of government alignment that CFIT has been careful to cultivate since receiving Treasury funding to take the project forward.

From grassroots campaign to institutional programme

The coalition’s origins lie in Project Nemo, a not-for-profit founded by Joanne Dewar and Kris Foster that spent more than two years building the evidence base for disability inclusion in financial services. Nationwide led a significant research publication through that initiative, identifying a structural gap: for people with learning disabilities or other conditions requiring assistance with day-to-day spending, the current system offers no practical midpoint. The choice, in effect, is between informal workarounds such as sharing cards, PINs and online banking credentials, or triggering disproportionately heavy legal arrangements designed for more serious incapacity.

CFIT launched the coalition formally at Money20/20 Europe in June 2026, and the addition of three of the UK’s largest retail banks gives it the institutional weight needed to move from research into implementation.

Anna Wallace, chief executive of CFIT, said: “For too many people, getting help to manage their money still means giving up more control than they should have to. Tackling that challenge requires coordinated action across the industry. CFIT is here to do exactly that: marshal the expertise, commitment and resources needed to move beyond recognising the problem to developing and testing practical solutions that deliver meaningful change.”

What the framework will do and when

Through the remainder of 2026, coalition participants will run focused sprints across two workstreams. The first is a Trust and Consent Framework, covering how individuals could appoint a trusted third party to assist with payments without a formal Power of Attorney, along with consent and permissioning models, liability considerations and regulatory alignment. The second workstream is a proof-of-concept pilot, potentially leveraging open banking infrastructure, to test supported payment journeys in real-world environments with consumers, carers and financial institutions. People with lived experience will be involved directly in designing and testing the proposed customer journey.

An interim report setting out the coalition’s initial findings and governance framework is expected before the end of the year. That will feed into a second phase focused on building and testing a minimum viable product for Supported Payments.

Regulatory and market context

The initiative sits within a broader UK push to make consumer financial services more inclusive. HM Treasury’s Financial Inclusion Strategy has previously cited the barriers faced by disabled consumers, and the FCA‘s Consumer Duty, which came into full force in 2023, places explicit obligations on firms to deliver good outcomes for customers in vulnerable circumstances. A Supported Payments framework would give banks a structured, regulated mechanism to meet those obligations rather than relying on informal accommodations that can expose both customer and institution to risk.

The open banking angle is worth watching. Using Payment Initiation Services or Account Information Services under the existing PSD2-derived framework in the UK could allow a trusted third party to initiate or oversee payments on behalf of a customer without requiring full account access, potentially resolving some of the consent and liability questions the coalition is working through. Whether that technical path proves sufficient, or whether primary legislation will be needed to establish the liability framework for trusted third parties, is likely to be a central question in the interim report.

title: The B2B payment stack wasn’t built for how businesses pay now
snippet: The B2B payment decision used to be binary. Legacy infrastructure still is.
fullText:
In 2024, ACH overtook checks  as the most common form of B2B payment in the U.S, but it took more than a century to get there. The Federal Reserve centralized check clearing around 1920. ACH came online in 1972 and spent 50 years catching up.

In the last decade alone, there’s been an exponential increase in payment modalities. Consumer payments gained Venmo, Zelle, Apple Pay, Cash App and tap-to-pay. B2B followed with its own set of new rails, each one adding a different set of fraud controls, settlement timing, remittance expectations and compliance rules. 

A single B2B relationship today might involve ACH, virtual card and check, all routing to different payees through different systems. For complex industries like healthcare and property and casualty, that mix shows up every day: one claim payout can route to a provider as ACH, a member as a prepaid card, and a contractor as a check, all off the same adjudication decision.

The payment mix is modern. The infrastructure moving it wasn’t built for how businesses pay now.

The decision set has expanded. Legacy infrastructure hasn’t. 

For most of the last century, the B2B payment decision was binary: check or ACH. 

Today, the decision set is vastly wider. ACH, real-time payments, virtual card, cross-border, embedded. Each with different fraud profiles, settlement timing, remittance expectations and compliance frameworks. Legacy infrastructure wasn’t built for any of them.

“The paper check problem” only makes it worse. When a legacy infrastructure can’t handle a modern payment type natively, the workaround carries its own cost: a separate vendor, manual process and parallel system someone has to maintain. This combined processing, postage and labor push the true cost of a check to $4, compared to $0.26–$0.50 for an ACH transaction. 

Fraud only compounds the problem further. In 2025, 76% of organizations were hit by payments fraud. Every new payment type an organization adds opens a new fraud vector that legacy controls weren’t built to catch.

Continuing to run modern payments on legacy infrastructure may seem like a cautious move, but it’s the riskier position, and it costs more the longer it stays.

Payments under pressure. 

The shift from checks to ACH is more than a one-year headline. Between 2015 and 2024, ACH’s share of B2B payments climbed from 25% to 41%, while check share fell from 32% to 13%.

The pressure is mounting, and it comes from the highest levels. In March 2025, the White House ordered federal agencies to stop issuing paper checks. The Treasury made the case in one line: checks are 16 times more likely to be lost, stolen or altered than a digital payment, and the paper infrastructure cost the federal government $657 million in FY2024. If the federal government can’t justify keeping checks, why should anyone else?

Regulation is closing in on the digital side, too. NACHA’s new rules for risk management, effective March 20, 2026, require real-time fraud prevention and detection on all outbound ACH payments. This now makes fraud prevention and security a required capability for payment infrastructure.  

Organizations face two infrastructure demands at once: meeting regulatory requirements for digital payments and responding to policy pressure to move away from paper. Legacy systems were not designed for those demands, making modernization harder to defer.

What legacy infrastructure can’t handle at scale 

Legacy B2B infrastructure was built around point-to-point payment flows rather than the full lifecycle, and this fragmented reality shows up in operations. In AP, a supplier calls about an invoice stuck in approval for 45 days; a controller discovers three vendor records point to the same TIN. In healthcare claims, a provider calls because a check for a resolved claim never arrived; the exception queue holds 200 items of unapplied payments and unposted remittances. 

Different industries, same breakdown: the people approving the payment and the people moving the money are working in different systems, with different vendors and the handoff between them is where cost accumulates.

That same handoff is where fraud finds its opening. BEC, vendor impersonation, bank account change attacks: each one targets the handoff between where a payment is decided and where the money moves. Legacy infrastructure wasn’t built to protect this blind spot, and modern fraud is sophisticated enough to exploit it.

What a modern B2B payment platform does differently

The scale of the fragmentation is already measurable. More than 90% of organizations use two or more payment vendors to run their payment lifecycle. 30% use four or more, and 55% say their systems don’t talk to each other. Proving that consolidation isn’t aspirational. It’s the obvious fix to a problem businesses are already quantifying. 

A modern B2B payment platform does one thing legacy infrastructure can’t: it owns the payment from the moment it’s decided to the moment it’s reconciled. One system, every payment type, end-to-end.

Every modern payment option runs through the same integration, so adding real-time payments or virtual card doesn’t mean another vendor contract. The payment partner holds and controls the payee payment preference, so the payer’s workflow doesn’t change but the payee experience does. Remittance travels with the money instead of chasing it and fraud monitoring runs against the full transaction history. And because the platform integrates directly with the core systems where AP, treasury and claims operations teams already work, nothing gets re-entered and no one switches tools to move a payment forward.

ECHO built their core platform for this exact architecture: one integration, full lifecycle visibility, multi-layered fraud prevention and security, and direct integrations with the core systems where finance and claims operations teams already work.

Payments aren’t moving back to binary. That leaves one question: Is the infrastructure moving your payments built for where B2B is going, or where it’s been?
